implementation_notes: kotlin-stdlib supplies the whole guard: `val res: Resource by lazy { acquire() }` delegates the property to a Lazy<T> whose first get() runs the initializer and remembers the result. The default LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED computes exactly once under a lock and publishes safely, PUBLICATION drops the lock (racing threads may all run the initializer and the first result wins) and NONE is for holders that never leave one thread. `lateinit var` only defers assignment - no initializer, no thread-safety guarantee, UninitializedPropertyAccessException on premature read - and suspending acquisition is written as a lazily started coroutine, `scope.async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { connect() }`, whose body runs on the first await. Where the classic form is still justified: a resource that must be closed or re-acquired cannot live in a Lazy - it is one-shot and holds a strong reference - so own it in a class with an explicit close()/refresh().
pitfalls: NONE is a foot-gun: nothing enforces the single-thread promise, so a shared holder initialized from a worker thread can be observed half-built; keep SYNCHRONIZED unless the value provably never crosses threads.
PUBLICATION may invoke the initializer more than once and discard the extra results - safe only for idempotent acquisition, because a second connection or file is created and immediately dropped.

A throwing initializer is not cached: Lazy returns to the uninitialized state and the next access runs the initializer again - the opposite of C# and Go, so a failing acquisition is retried on every access with no backoff.

lateinit is not a lazy resource holder: reading before assignment throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException, there is no visibility guarantee across threads, and it cannot hold nullable or primitive types.
